ai.question: A high-school student asks ChatGPT to write the code for a programming-class project. The code runs, the project gets an A. A year later the student tries to extend the project and discovers the variable names made no sense and the logic was wrong in two places. What's the realistic lesson?
ai.answer: AI-generated code that runs is not the same as code you understand — you owe a careful read-through before turning it in, because tomorrow you will be the one stuck with it.
choices: AI-generated code that runs is not the same as code you understand — you owe a careful read-through before turning it in, because tomorrow you will be the one stuck with it.
AI-generated code is never wrong if it runs the first time — a working test result proves the code is logically correct and ready to be submitted for credit.
AI-generated code becomes the student's legal property automatically — no school can fairly grade work that the chatbot produced on the student's behalf.
AI-generated code is always written by stealing from open-source repositories — every project handed in this way is grounds for academic dishonesty proceedings.
ai.context: Large language models are pattern-completion engines. They produce code that looks like working code from their training data, but they have no understanding of the specific problem being solved. The output often runs and even passes a graded rubric, while containing variable names that don't match the domain, logic that handles only the common path, or subtle bugs that don't trigger on the test input. The recognition skill: AI assistance shifts the cost of understanding the code from writing-time to maintenance-time. The student who didn't read the AI's output carefully is the same student who can't fix it a year later.

ai.question: Researchers in 2023 and 2024 documented several browser extensions that were initially benign and then became malicious after the developer sold the extension or was compromised. The extensions had already been installed by millions of users. What's the defensive lesson?
ai.answer: Periodically audit installed extensions and remove ones you don't actively use — long-tail extensions are a known supply-chain risk
choices: Periodically audit installed extensions and remove ones you don't actively use — long-tail extensions are a known supply-chain risk
Install only one extension at a time — running multiple extensions makes supply-chain attacks impossible
Use only paid extensions — paid extensions cannot be compromised or sold to malicious developers
Use only Chrome extensions — Firefox and Edge extensions are far more vulnerable to supply-chain compromise
ai.context: The browser-extension supply chain has been targeted repeatedly. The Cyberhaven incident in December 2024 saw a popular extension's developer accounts compromised and a malicious update pushed to users. Earlier cases included Great Suspender (sold to a new owner who inserted ad-tracking) and numerous shopping extensions that became data-exfiltration tools. Browser extensions you don't actively use are an attack surface for nothing in return. Defensive routine: open chrome://extensions or about:addons every few months; remove anything you haven't used in 60 days; for the ones you keep, check the last-updated date and reviewer activity. Apply the same principle to mobile apps with broad permissions you don't use.

ai.question: Sam Altman flew to Saudi Arabia and the UAE in 2024 to pitch a multi-trillion-dollar AI chip-fab plan. Within a year, sovereign wealth funds — UAE's MGX, Saudi PIF, Singapore's Temasek — were investors in major US AI firms and founding partners in OpenAI's Stargate compute project. What's the kid's recognition?
ai.answer: Foreign government capital is now embedded in major US AI firms — that does not automatically compromise these companies, but it creates real dependencies and influence relationships worth watching
choices: Foreign government capital is now embedded in major US AI firms — that does not automatically compromise these companies, but it creates real dependencies and influence relationships worth watching
Federal law strictly bars all foreign government investment in any US AI company — sovereign-wealth stakes in this sector are forbidden by statute and impossible in practice in any quarter
No foreign sovereign-wealth fund holds any stake in any frontier US AI company — Stargate was funded purely by domestic venture capital and Microsoft cloud credits with no other capital sources
Every frontier US AI lab is majority-owned by a foreign sovereign-wealth fund — domestic investors have been entirely displaced from the sector by foreign governments in every disclosure today
ai.context: MGX (UAE) was a founding partner in the Stargate compute investment announced January 2025. Saudi PIF has signaled major AI ambitions tied to its Vision 2030 plan. CFIUS — the Committee on Foreign Investment in the US — reviews some of these transactions with a mixed track record. Recognition skill: the politics of AI is not purely domestic. Foreign investors with their own government's interests are part of the capital stack, and that shapes what these companies can and cannot do.

ai.question: Most of the AI a kid uses today came out of military research grants. DARPA paid for ARPANET (which became the Internet), the Stanford AI Lab's early work, computer-vision and natural-language-processing programs through the 1980s, and the PhD pipeline that trained the researchers now running OpenAI, Anthropic, and DeepMind. What is the recognition?
ai.answer: Modern frontier AI is partly a return on decades of public investment in basic research — but the value capture flows mostly to a few private firms, which raises real questions about the public's stake in the outcome
choices: Modern frontier AI is partly a return on decades of public investment in basic research — but the value capture flows mostly to a few private firms, which raises real questions about the public's stake in the outcome
Modern frontier AI is purely private from start to finish — no government funding ever contributed to any foundational AI research anywhere in the world at any point in the field's history

Modern frontier AI was developed in roughly three years from scratch — no decades-long research history preceded the rise of contemporary deep-learning systems used at any current frontier lab worldwide
Modern frontier AI is fully publicly owned by the United States — every model from every major lab is the legal property of the US federal government under existing intellectual-property statute
ai.context: This pattern repeats across other federally-funded technologies. The Internet, GPS, the touchscreen interface, and major drug classes (mRNA among them) trace lineages to NIH, NSF, DOD, and DOE research dollars. The current value capture in AI flows to a small number of private firms — partly through patents, partly through compute moats, partly through talent concentration. Recognition skill: the standard 'private innovation' framing obscures the long public-investment lineage, and the politics of who reaps the resulting upside is a live, unresolved question.

grammar.question: The English legal term 'subpoena' — a court order to appear and testify — comes from Latin. What does 'sub poena' literally mean, and what does that reveal about the writ's force?
grammar.answer: 'Under penalty' — sub (under) + poena (punishment). The writ commands appearance UNDER the threat of being penalized for non-appearance.
choices: 'Under penalty' — sub (under) + poena (punishment). The writ commands appearance UNDER the threat of being penalized for non-appearance.
'In secret' — sub (under) + poena (whisper). The Roman practice of confidential testimony.
'Below the throne' — sub (under) + poena (royal seat). The writ was sealed at the level of the throne.
'After the deed' — sub (after) + poena (verdict). The summons could only be issued post-judgment.
grammar.context: 'Subpoena' = Latin 'sub' (under) + 'poena' (penalty, punishment) = 'under penalty.' The writ was so named because its opening Latin formula warned the recipient that non-appearance would result in penalty — fine or imprisonment. The full traditional phrase was 'sub poena centum librarum' ('under penalty of one hundred pounds'). The Greek 'poine' (punishment) is the same root and gave English 'punish' (via Latin 'punire') and 'pain' (via Old French — 'pain' originally meant 'punishment'). One Latin word 'poena' branched into three English words. Other legal Latin in everyday English: 'pro bono' (for good), 'amicus curiae' (friend of the court), 'res ipsa loquitur' (the thing speaks for itself), 'mens rea' (a guilty mind), 'actus reus' (a guilty act). The law's vocabulary is itself a Latin code.

history.question: In 1953-54, with the Cold War deepening and McCarthy hearings raging, J. Robert Oppenheimer — Manhattan Project scientific director, Trinity test hero, former AEC adviser — was investigated by a personnel security board over his opposition to the hydrogen bomb program (he had favored arms control), past leftist associations (his brother Frank was an ex-Communist), and 1943 statements about Soviet contacts. The board found him 'loyal' but a 'security risk' and revoked his clearance on June 29, 1954. What was the broader significance?
history.answer: It signaled that even decorated scientific service did not protect against ideological investigation in Cold War America
choices: It signaled that even decorated scientific service did not protect against ideological investigation in Cold War America
It established the principle that all federal scientific advisers must publicly endorse current weapons programs
It eliminated civilian advisers from the AEC structure, transferring authority entirely to military officials
It prompted Congress to pass a law requiring loyalty oaths from all federally funded scientific researchers
history.context: Oppenheimer's clearance revocation ended his role in nuclear policy. He spent the rest of his career at the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton, dying in 1967 of throat cancer. In December 2022, the U.S. Department of Energy formally vacated the 1954 decision, calling it the product of a 'flawed process.' Edward Teller, who had testified against Oppenheimer, was ostracized by much of the physics community for the rest of his life. Christopher Nolan's 2023 film Oppenheimer renewed broad public engagement with the episode.

philosophy.question: The 'inverted spectrum' thought experiment: imagine you and a friend both call fire engines 'red' and grass 'green' — but what you see looking at fire is what she sees looking at grass, and vice versa. No behavior would catch the difference. What does this case expose?
philosophy.answer: What experiences FEEL like may not be fixed by behavior — two people could match in word and act yet differ in inner color experience.
choices: What experiences FEEL like may not be fixed by behavior — two people could match in word and act yet differ in inner color experience.
The case is a pseudo-question — since no behavior would distinguish them, there is no real fact about which one is inverted.
Inner experience IS brain activity — the brains are identical by stipulation, so the inverts cannot occur in the first place.
Color words have no real meaning — since people might see colors differently, words like 'red' are empty labels with no shared content.
philosophy.context: John Locke (Essay Concerning Human Understanding, 1689, Book II ch. 32) raised the inverted spectrum to ask whether qualia — what experiences are LIKE — can be pinned down by behavior. Modern revivals (Shoemaker 1981, Block 1990) press the case against functionalism, the view that mental states ARE their causal-functional roles.

science.question: On the ocean, people watching a ship sail far away see it disappear BOTTOM FIRST below the horizon. What does that tell us about Earth's shape?
science.answer: Earth is a sphere, not a flat disk
choices: Earth is a sphere, not a flat disk
Ships shrink as they go far away
The sea slowly pulls ships under
Light can't travel across oceans
science.context: Ancient Greek thinkers like Eratosthenes (around 240 BC) figured out Earth was round and measured its size well using shadows. Ships disappearing hull-first, the round shadow Earth casts on the Moon during eclipses, and photos from space all confirm it.

science.question: In 1633 Galileo was tried for saying Earth goes around the Sun. The experts mocked him; he was right. Lesson?
science.answer: Big experts can be wrong for a while
choices: Big experts can be wrong for a while
Outsiders are always wrong on nature
Books are not meant to be checked
Experts all say the same things always
science.context: Galileo Galilei (1564-1642) used a telescope to discover Jupiter's moons, the phases of Venus, and craters on the Moon. His 1632 book defended the Sun-centered view first argued by Copernicus. The Roman Inquisition tried him in 1633 and forced him to publicly recant — but the Sun really is at the center of our solar system, and history remembers him as right.

science.question: When researcher Andrew Montford and others examined the original abstracts coded by Cook et al. in their 2013 paper, they found that many papers categorized as 'endorsing' the consensus actually took no clear position on human attribution — they simply assumed warming and studied its effects. What's the methodological lesson?
science.answer: How researchers code 'endorsement' determines the headline number — methodological choices that drive a 97% claim deserve published scrutiny, not deference
choices: How researchers code 'endorsement' determines the headline number — methodological choices that drive a 97% claim deserve published scrutiny, not deference
Coding methodology is irrelevant in literature surveys — a position now universally accepted in the climate-research community across the world
Cook published every coding decision for public review — a transparency standard rarely matched by any other field of empirical research
Critical reanalysis of climate papers is impossible — a procedural rule established by major climate-publishing journals over the last decade
science.context: Cook et al. used volunteers to categorize abstracts using a 7-point scale. Tol's reanalysis (2014, *Energy Policy*) found inconsistencies in the coding and concluded the headline 97% claim was not robust. Cook responded with defenses of the methodology. The substantive lesson: large literature-survey claims need methodology scrutiny — and 'consensus' figures depend on what question was actually being asked.

trivia.question: Released in 1989, Jim Henson's character Yoda from Star Wars (1980) gets a brief 'Empire Strikes Back' Easter-egg appearance in Indiana Jones and the Last Crusade (1989) during the Berlin book-burning scene. The two characters share a creator connection. What's the specific connection?
trivia.answer: Frank Oz performed Yoda's voice and puppetry for ESB and the Last Crusade scene used the same Oz vocal style for a brief gag
choices: Frank Oz performed Yoda's voice and puppetry for ESB and the Last Crusade scene used the same Oz vocal style for a brief gag
Stuart Freeborn designed both Yoda's makeup and a Nazi officer's prosthetic for Last Crusade
Industrial Light & Magic built both Yoda's puppetry rig and Last Crusade's Holy Grail effect
The hidden Yoda appears as a ghost on a flag in the Berlin book-burning crowd scene
trivia.context: Stuart Freeborn was the legendary Empire makeup designer who built Yoda's original puppet. He also worked on Star Wars (1977) doing the Mos Eisley aliens. Indiana Jones and the Last Crusade has many Easter eggs — Indiana Jones's name on a Yale University football team list, the Lucasfilm 'C-3PO' relief carving in the Petra temple, and the Mickey Mouse on Indy's tie in the airport scene. Star Wars cameos in Indy films had been a tradition since Raiders.
